newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - Feb 11.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - Feb 11.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories Tuesday:
* Apple Computer said it expects to report a substantial loss this quarter because of charges that include restructuring costs and a $322 million write-off for acquiring Next Software Inc.
* The dollar was mixed in its first trading day after G7 officials agreed that the currency had risen high enough.
* Tokyo stocks rose 1.8 percent after the G7 accord, and Germany's DAX index rose 1.5 percent.
* The yield on the 30-year bond was unchanged at 6.70 percent.
* Westinghouse Electric agreed to acquire Gaylord Entertainment's two major cable networks -- the Nashville Network and Country Music Television -- for $1.55 billion in stock.
* Richard Jalkut, head of NYNEX's telecommunications unit, said he would resign after the company merges with Bell Atlantic because he does not want the job he was offered in the combined entity.
* The Dow industrials fell 49.26 to close at 6,806.54, and the Nasdaq composite fell 22.37 to 1,335.34.
* 3Com fell 13-1/2 to 37-1/4 after it said its fiscal third quarter results would be below analysts expectations.
* Mercury Finance said it had secured a $50 million short-term loan from the Bank of America.
* The Council of Economic Advisers said in a new report that the gap between the country's rich and poor appears to have stopped widening and may have reversed.

* The $108 billion state pension fund of California has included Apple, Reebok, Novell, Bassett Furniture, Fleming Cos Inc, Rollins Environmental, Sensormatic Electronics, Stride Rite, Summit Technology and Sybase in its list of underperfoming stocks.
* A Federal judge gave final approval to class-action settlements that will pay 68.9 million to investors who claim to have been defrauded by Ivan Boesky and others in 1980s trading scandals.
* Readers Digest plans to begin selling advertising on its back cover.
* Yahoo and other Internet search companies have been building brand awareness through television and radio advertising.
* A group of market watchers calling themselves the New Era say U.S. stock prices are not over-valued when judged under adjusted criteria, but traditionalsts still rely on the lessons of history.

* Bruce Wasserstein and Joseph Perella gained fame during the 1980s takeovers and are again the center of attention, with Wasserstein advising Dean Witter as the company prepares to merge with Morgan Stanley, where Perella is the head of investment banking.
